title: Episode 37: The Great Serum Run of 1925: Balto, Togo, and the Iditarod

In January 1925, a deadly diphtheria epidemic broke out among the children of Nome, Alaska, isolated by sea ice and subzero blizzards. With airplanes grounded by frozen engines, twenty Native and Norwegian dog mushers and 150 sled dogs formed an emergency relay across 674 miles of the treacherous Iditarod Trail, delivering the life-saving serum in five and a half days.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the dead of winter in nineteen twenty-five, the isolated coastal town of Nome, Alaska was cut off from the rest of the world. Bering Sea ice had locked the harbor in a frozen grip for the winter, and howling subarctic blizzards plunged temperatures to fifty degrees below zero. In January, the town's lone physician, Dr. Curtis Welch, made a terrifying diagnosis: diphtheria, a deadly, highly contagious respiratory infection known as the 'strangling angel,' was spreading rapidly among the town's children. Nome's entire supply of antitoxin was expired, and without fresh serum, the entire population of ten thousand was threatened with annihilation. With aviation impossible due to primitive open-cockpit planes that could not fly in the Arctic cold, salvation rested entirely on the courage of twenty sled dog drivers and one hundred and fifty Siberian huskies in a desperate, six-hundred-and-seventy-four-mile race against death. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE STRANGLING ANGEL IN NOME
In January nineteen twenty-five, Nome, Alaska was an isolated, frozen subarctic outpost of two thousand permanent residents, surrounded by another ten thousand Native Inupiat villagers scattered along the Seward Peninsula. The town had no roads or rail connections to the outside world; during the eight long months of winter, its only lifeline to the south was a single telegraph wire. On January twentieth, Dr. Curtis Welch was summoned to examine several sick Inupiat children. When he looked down their throats, his heart sank with dread: a thick, grayish membrane covered their tonsils and windpipes. It was diphtheria—a terrifying, highly infectious bacterial disease that suffocated victims to death. Two children had already died, and several more were desperately ill. Dr. Welch checked the hospital pharmacy and found that Nome's entire supply of diphtheria antitoxin serum had expired six years earlier, and a fresh order sent to Seattle had failed to arrive before the harbor froze over. Knowing that Native populations possessed zero natural immunity and that the disease had a near one-hundred-percent fatality rate without serum, Dr. Welch fired off an urgent, frantic telegram to the U.S. Public Health Service in Washington: 'An epidemic of diphtheria is almost inevitable here. I am in urgent need of one million units of diphtheria antitoxin. Mail is only possible form of transportation. Diphtheria antitoxin is only hope of saving children.' Isolated on the frozen edge of the Bering Sea, Nome twenty-five hundred residents had no road or rail link to the outside world, depending entirely on dog teams once winter ice locked the harbor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GREAT ARCTIC DILEMMA
The desperate telegram triggered emergency conferences in Washington and Alaska. A supply of three hundred thousand units of antitoxin was located in a hospital in Anchorage. But how to transport the fragile glass ampoules over a thousand miles of frozen wilderness to Nome? The package could be carried by the Alaska Railroad three hundred miles north to the railhead at Nenana, but from Nenana to Nome lay six hundred and seventy-four miles of trackless, subarctic wilderness along the historic Iditarod mail trail. Territorial Governor Scott Bone explored using two open-cockpit biplanes stationed in Fairbanks, but veteran bush pilots warned that in temperatures of fifty degrees below zero, the plane's liquid-cooled radiators would freeze solid in mid-air, the fragile wings would ice up, and a crash was virtually guaranteed. Furthermore, the fragile liquid serum would freeze, shatter the glass vials, and lose all its medical potency if exposed to the subarctic cold. Governor Bone made the fateful executive decision: the serum would be transported by what had never failed in the Arctic: an emergency dog sled relay, manned by the finest Athabascan Native and Norwegian mushers in Alaska. Dr. Curtis Welch watched in horror as four Native children succumbed to the suffocating membrane of diphtheria, knowing his entire supply of antitoxin was expired and useless against an epidemic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RELAY BEGINS AT NENANA
On the night of January twenty-seventh, nineteen twenty-five, the passenger train pulled into the snow-covered depot at Nenana. Conductor Frank Cassidy handed a twenty-pound, quilt-wrapped package wrapped in waterproof canvas to the first musher, Wild Bill Shannon. The thermometer at the depot registered fifty degrees below zero and was falling rapidly. Shannon hitched his team of nine half-breed malamutes, checked the leather bindings on the sled, and set off into the black Arctic night along the frozen Tanana River. The cold was so intense that Shannon's breath froze into ice on his face, his lungs burned with every breath, and four of his dogs suffered frozen lungs and later died. After fifty-two grueling miles, Shannon reached Tolovana with blackened, frostbitten facial skin, handing the serum to the next musher. Over the next three days, the precious package was passed from musher to musher like an Olympic baton: Dan Green, Johnny Folger, Sam Joseph, Titus Nikolai, Harry Pitka, and Bill McCarty. Traveling through howling blizzards and over treacherous overflow ice on the Yukon River, the mushers averaged an astonishing seven miles an hour in temperatures that hovered between forty and sixty-two degrees below zero. Governor Scott Bone organized the historic dog team relay from Nenana along the frozen Tanana and Yukon rivers, selecting the finest mushers and canine athletes in northern history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: LEONHARD SEPPALA AND TOGO
The most perilous and heroic leg of the relay was assigned to the undisputed king of Alaskan dog mushing: forty-seven-year-old Norwegian-born Leonhard Seppala, and his legendary twelve-year-old lead dog, a small Siberian husky named Togo. While other mushers covered twenty to thirty miles each, Seppala set out from Nome to meet the relay, covering a staggering two hundred and sixty miles across the most dangerous terrain on Earth. Meeting musher Henry Ivanoff at Shaktoolik, Seppala secured the serum and turned his team back into the teeth of an eighty-mile-per-hour gale wind that plunged the windchill to an unimaginable eighty-five degrees below zero. To save an entire day of travel, Seppala took a daring, life-or-death gamble: he drove his team directly across the frozen, buckled sea ice of Norton Sound, rather than taking the safe overland detour around the coastline. The ice of Norton Sound was shifting, groaning, and cracking beneath the blizzard; at any moment, the ice sheet could break away from the mainland and drift into the open Arctic ocean. Togo, relying on sheer instinct and extraordinary courage, navigated through pitch-black darkness, leaping across open leads of freezing seawater and guiding the team safely across twenty miles of shattering sea ice just hours before the entire ice field broke up and drifted to sea. Wild Bill Shannon sprinted into the subzero dark at sixty degrees below zero, suffering frostbite that blackened his face as his huskies dashed across the ice along the river corridor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: BALTO AND THE FINAL PUSH IN THE DARK
Seppala handed the serum to Charlie Olson, who braved blinding gales to deliver it to Gunnar Kaasen at Bluff on the evening of February first. Kaasen hitched a team of dogs from Seppala's kennel, anchored by a sturdy, black six-year-old Siberian husky named Balto. By the time Kaasen set out, the blizzard was raging at peak fury. The blowing snow was so thick that Kaasen could not even see his wheel dogs harnessed immediately in front of his sled. Driven by howling winds, the sled flipped over in a deep snowdrift near Topkok, spilling the precious package into the snow. In a panic, Kaasen took off his heavy beaver mittens and desperately clawed through the freezing drifts with his bare hands in the dark, his fingers turning white with frostbite, until he felt the canvas package intact. Continuing forward, Kaasen reached the roadhouse at Safety at three o'clock in the morning on February second. The next scheduled musher, Ed Rohn, was asleep, assuming Kaasen had stopped due to the storm. Rather than waste precious hours waking Rohn and harnessing a fresh team, Kaasen and Balto pushed on through the final twenty-one miles. Leonhard Seppala trusted his twelve-year-old lead dog Togo to navigate shifting pack ice in pitch-black gale winds across Norton Sound, cutting eighty miles off the route in one of the greatest feats of mushing ever recorded.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: SALVATION IN NOME AT DAWN
At five-thirty in the morning on Monday, February second, nineteen twenty-five, Gunnar Kaasen's sled slid to a halt on Front Street in Nome. The team had covered the final grueling miles in sub-zero dark. Kaasen collapsed into the snow, so exhausted he could barely speak, and crawled to Balto's side, weeping as he pulled icy splinters from the dog's paws and whispering: 'Damn fine dog.' The six-hundred-and-seventy-four-mile journey, which normally required twenty-five days by territorial mail sled, had been completed in an astonishing five and a half days—one hundred and twenty-seven hours—establishing a world record. Dr. Welch thawed the serum, administered it to the infected children, and within days, the epidemic was broken; not a single additional child died. The news flashed across global wire services, and an anxious world celebrated the deliverance of the children of Nome. Gunnar Kaasen and Balto pushed through blinding ground blizzards where Kaasen could not see his hand before his face, arriving in Nome at dawn to deliver the life-saving serum intact.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: CENTRAL PARK, TOGO'S JUSTICE, AND THE IDITAROD
The Serum Run captured the hearts of millions across the globe. Ten months later, a magnificent bronze statue of Balto was unveiled in New York City's Central Park, dedicated to the indomitable spirit of the sled dogs. While Balto received immediate celebrity, canine historians later recognized that Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog Togo had carried the serum over the longest, most perilous leg—ninety-one miles through eighty-mile-per-hour winds and cracking sea ice, compared to Balto's fifty-three miles. In recent years, Togo's legendary leadership has been immortalized with his own bronze statue in Seward Park in Manhattan, a Hollywood feature film, and recognition as the greatest sled dog in history. In nineteen seventy-three, the historic route was commemorated permanently with the creation of the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, honoring both Native and Norwegian mushers. The Great Serum Run of 1925 remains an immortal testament to the unbreakable bond between humans and dogs, and the boundless courage that triumphs over the harshest forces of nature. The heroic run inspired the founding of the legendary Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, ensuring that the courage of the mushers and their devoted canine companions remains celebrated across the globe.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Great Serum Run of 1925 is a shining beacon of selflessness, endurance, and inter-species loyalty. It proves that in the darkest, coldest nights of life, courage and love will always find a way through the storm. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we explore another extraordinary chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.
